episode_title: Episode 045 - What does it take to lead strategically?

real_qa.q: What is the balcony and dance floor philosophy in strategic leadership?
real_qa.r: The balcony and dance floor philosophy represents the balance of where leaders spend their time. The dance floor is operational work—handling daily problems, production issues, and immediate concerns. The balcony is stepping back to view operations from 10,000 or 30,000 feet, identifying bottlenecks, and planning strategically for the next year. Strategic leadership requires spending more time on the balcony developing the next level of leaders so the organization runs well whether the leader is present or not.

real_qa.q: What are the signs that a leader has become a bottleneck for their organization?
real_qa.r: Key signs include: constantly being on vacation or days off while answering texts and emails, feeling like they accomplished nothing despite a stressful day of problem-solving, running around putting out fires like 'a chicken with their head cut off,' and having an open-door policy where everyone comes to them for answers rather than developing their own problem-solving skills. If the leader must be present all the time, they are not developing other leaders and are not being strategic.

real_qa.q: Why do competent managers struggle to develop people around them?
real_qa.r: Competent managers struggle because they receive a dopamine hit when they solve problems—people praise them and they feel they are doing their job well. Most manager job descriptions emphasize solving problems and ensuring product flow rather than strategic development. Additionally, open-door policies create dependency: employees seek out the expert for answers, and even though the manager's intentions are good, they end up disempowering employees who need to learn problem-solving themselves. The manager becomes 'the guru' and everyone else becomes just 'hands and feet.'
real_qa.requete: why competent managers fail develop employees

real_qa.q: What was the $20 mission statement challenge Jimmy Nelson used in leadership classes?
real_qa.r: In leadership classes over 20 years, Dr. Nelson offered $20 from his wallet to anyone who could recite their organization's mission statement word for word. In all those years, he has never paid a dime. Leaders attempt but cannot deliver the exact mission, revealing that if leaders themselves don't know the mission, frontline employees definitely won't, leading to decisions that contradict organizational purpose.

real_qa.q: How did connecting a stamping machine operator to the brake component she produced impact her engagement?
real_qa.r: A woman making a small bracket for Ram truck brake systems initially said 'I don't know, don't care. I just make 10,000 of them and off I go.' When the engineer explained her bracket held the braking system and brake failure could occur without quality, her perspective changed. She posted a graphic showing the truck and highlighted brake system location above her workstation. Her engagement transformed from meaningless repetition to understanding she was making a part critical for driver safety, changing how she discussed her work with family and friends.
